summary.text: An eclipsing binary is a pair of stars whose orbit lies in a plane along our line of sight, so the stars eclipse and transit each other.
Because the stars pass in front of one another, the pair changes in brightness, and that change is how such a pair is detected.
Eclipsing binaries belong to the photometric binaries, and a pair can fit several observing classes at once.

items.prompt: Using only measurements of how much light arrives over time, what pattern points to an eclipsing binary?

options.label: Brightness dips as one star passes in front of the other
A single star's position drifting as an unseen partner tugs it
Two separate points of light visible through a telescope
A steady brightness that never changes at all

items.explain: Eclipsing binaries are detected photometrically, by changes in brightness caused by an eclipse.

items.prompt: A pair of stars is known to be an eclipsing binary. Can it also be classified another way?

options.label: No, every binary belongs to just one class
No, an eclipse rules out every other method
Yes, some are also spectroscopic binaries
Yes, but only if the two stars match in brightness

Visual binaries
Spectroscopic binaries
Astrometric binaries

items.prompt: No one can put a lone star on a scale. What do binary stars like these let astronomers do?

options.label: Count the planets around each star
Photograph the surface of each star

By brightness changes from an eclipse, not by seeing two stars

paragraphs.heading: Stars that block each other
paragraphs.text: A binary star is two stars bound by gravity and orbiting each other; more strictly, the pair revolves around a shared center of mass. Sometimes the plane of that orbit happens to lie along our line of sight. Then, seen from Earth, the two stars take turns passing in front of each other, eclipsing and transiting. A pair like this is called an eclipsing binary.

paragraphs.heading: Found by its light
paragraphs.text: Astronomers sort binaries by the way they are observed, and eclipsing pairs belong to the photometric group: binaries noticed through changes in brightness caused by an eclipse. That group also takes in other binaries whose brightness changes as they orbit. The other groups are visual binaries, which a telescope can split into two stars; spectroscopic binaries, revealed by periodic changes in spectral lines; and astrometric binaries, revealed when a star's position shifts because of an unseen companion.

paragraphs.heading: One pair, many labels
paragraphs.text: These groups overlap. Any binary star can belong to more than one of them, and several spectroscopic binaries are also eclipsing binaries. So the same pair might both dim during its eclipses and show periodic changes in its spectral lines. By contrast, many visual binaries take centuries or millennia to complete one orbit, so their orbits are uncertain or poorly known.

paragraphs.heading: Why such pairs matter
paragraphs.text: Binary stars rank among the most important objects in astrophysics. They let astronomers measure the masses of stars directly and test theories of how stars evolve. When the two stars are close, their gravity can distort each other's outer atmospheres. In some cases they even swap mass, pushing their evolution into stages a single star cannot reach.

paragraphs.heading: Binaries in the wider sky
paragraphs.text: Binaries are common at the centers of many planetary nebulae, and they are where both novae and type Ia supernovae come from. Familiar binaries include Sirius and Cygnus X-1, a well-known black hole. Not every pair that looks close is a real binary, though. Two stars can appear side by side in the sky while lying at vastly different distances from the Sun; these are called optical doubles.
